articles.title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
articles.author: Alina Selyukh
articles.body_markdown:
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.

A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.

It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.

The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.

Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.

The line of credit never came.

"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."

For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.

### A business in need

Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.

Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.

Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.

Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.

Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.

"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."

By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.

Booking his biggest tour yet, with a 1980s German superstar, Shahinian sought his fifth round of Amex merchant funding.

Except this time, Amex said no. The company was phasing out the program.

All Shahinian could think was: "Whoa." Tours are costly affairs with down payments to venues, marketing, airfare, lights and sound. He'd left himself no time to maneuver — two weeks to acquire about $200,000.

Enter merchant cash advances.

### A funding void

Small businesses in the U.S. consistently say they turn to merchant cash advances, MCAs, because they find few alternatives, especially in an emergency.

Most traditional lending takes months and vigorous vetting. The Small Business Administration has tightened its lending rules. Big banks reject about 20% of business loan applications, according to the Treasury Department, and respond to a quarter with only partial funding. A recent Federal Reserve survey found even lower odds.

MCAs, by contrast, present themselves as a lifeline, offering large sums within hours.

Their fees, however, run from 25% to 200% and more, when translated into an annual rate. MCA firms argue they charge a lot because they take on big risks.

They also face almost no regulatory oversight.

MCAs escape most lending laws because, technically, they are not loans. An MCA is meant to be a purchase of future sales — a business gets cash in exchange for a steady cut of its earnings later. MCA funders generally aren't required to be licensed and face no legal limit to how much they can charge.

The industry runs the gamut: A funder could be a firm recommended by Amazon, or the latest fintech startup, or a former subprime mortgage lender. Some rely on brokers to drum up deals. Most collect payment by withdrawing directly from their borrowers' bank accounts — often daily.

Shahinian, scrambling after the Amex rejection, lined up two cash advances for a total of $250,000, he says, owing back almost $400,000. This saved his concert tour but cost him all the profits.

"It was my fault — I waited last minute," Shahinian says. "I'm talking to myself, 'Vahe, you had to do it this time. You're never going back to MCAs.'"

### A fateful offer

But MCA pitches never stop. Sometimes, Shahinian replied that he wanted only a traditional loan, something along an 8% interest rate.

Before he even went hunting, the offer came to him — the pitch that changed his life: The line of credit up to $750,000 at an annual interest rate just under 9%. Finally, Shahinian thought, someone recognized the quality of his business.

"It's like the puzzle fit, you know?" he says.

This encounter took Shahinian beyond the MCAs' unforgiving fees into what he alleges was fraud.

As he weighed the offer's condition — 30 days of daily $3,600 payments — he didn't recognize it as a merchant cash advance.

On the phone, the broker presented it as a routine test, Shahinian says, to show his dependability before he'd qualify for his preapproved line of credit. Shahinian had no lawyer or adviser to consult then. He looked up the finance firm, Wall Street-based EIN Cap; it advertised itself as a "provider of working capital to local businesses."

"I was assured that 'We've done this for years. We don't care about a 30-day program — our goal is long term,'" Shahinian says. "The whole setup was to make someone like me feel assured, feel safe — and I felt safe to go in it."

From the start, Shahinian says, he received $228,000 instead of the promised $250,000. The difference was withheld as an initial fee, a common feature of MCAs. He set aside almost half the funds to secure his daily $3,600 payment. The rest vanished into down payments for venues and other tour investments.

After 30 days, when the line of credit didn't materialize, Shahinian says the broker portrayed the delays as technical. His emails grew urgent.

"I had calculated and planned everything based on the 30-day plan."

"I planned massive tour projects based on this solid word. This is not a joke."

"I don't think you understand the urgency of this situation. I'm basically out of time."

EIN Cap later in court argued it never promised Shahinian any loans or lines of credit — only a merchant cash advance, which it delivered. EIN Cap said it was the brokers — the middlemen — who had arranged the deal and made promises. Much of what the company had to say about its ties to those brokers is in sealed depositions.

After 40 days of daily payments, Shahinian says, for the first time, his bank account hit zero.

### A spiral of debt

Shahinian's lawyer, Shane Heskin — who has been clashing with MCA companies for a decade — calls what happened here "carroting." As in, a carrot gets dangled in front of a small-business owner in the form of an attractive financing deal — a low-interest loan — in a bait and switch to sign an unsolicited MCA.

"I see two or three a week," Heskin says about such cases. "They're exploding."

Heskin says common targets are first-time business owners, first-time borrowers and especially immigrants.

NPR spoke with several entrepreneurs who were "carroted" in similar ways. One described falling into a deep depression; another declared bankruptcy. None, except Shahinian, wanted to speak on the record.

Shahinian says he paid his unwanted MCA to the end, hemorrhaging cash.

"That's just who I am, you know?" he says, explaining his choice. "Who I was."

In fact, had he stopped paying, his funders might have sued him for debt collection — a common consequence with MCAs.

Days before his biggest concert tour yet, with his accounts empty, Shahinian assessed costs: venues still half-paid, airfare unbooked and rising in price, thousands of tickets undermarketed and unsold.

He did what many business owners do when they struggle to stay afloat with merchant cash advances: He took out more cash advances.

### A collapse

Shahinian says his two new MCAs, totaling around $250,000, evaporated into expenses in half a day.

"From here," he says, "the avalanche of money over money, over money, over money started."

He tapped his credit and then home equity — his own, his parents' and his best friend's. Within weeks, Shahinian says, he was more than $1 million in debt to friends and family.

"He asked me for some money, and, I mean, I could see he's drowning, you know?" says Zorik Yeghikian, who did lend to Shahinian later on. He's a restaurant owner whom Shahinian had helped win a catering contract for a local concert venue.

Yeghikian knew the trap of MCA payments. They had nearly capsized his own business, he says, when he'd borrowed about $30,000 and owed nearly triple. Yeghikian slept at his restaurant and worked double shifts alongside his wife, both forgoing pay.

"I lost my hair," Yeghikian says. "I went through hell those years."

The exact scale of the MCA industry is unclear, but it's ballooning. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City reports that businesses are increasingly turning to MCAs to cover basic expenses like payroll. MCAs are a frequent feature in small-business bankruptcies, which have been rising.

Shahinian canceled several concerts of his tours, costing him six-figure losses. Many shows went underpromoted and undersold. They might have seemed OK to the audience but did little to save him.

He began to default on his debts.

Shahinian watched himself become someone who lost count of overdue bills and unpaid invoices. He tapped more emergency MCAs and raked in collections notices. Some of his clients received lien letters, asking them to redirect any payments meant for Shahinian to his funders instead. His business relationships wore thin. His social circle shrunk.

He huddled in his home office with his tuxedo cats, Koby and Toby, and faced the existential dilemma: fight or flight?

### A fight or a fold

Shahinian's choice — to fight — is rare. Borrowers often struggle to afford lawyers, let alone find one familiar with the MCA industry.

And MCA firms can be difficult to pin down. Shahinian says he had to hire a private investigator to reach his funders to serve his lawsuit.

He sued EIN Cap and the brokers in 2019. Three years later, he settled his claims against the brokers to focus on EIN. His remaining case in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles accuses EIN of fraud.

"EIN Cap denies Mr. Shahinian's claims, and its position is set out in its public court filings," Levi Silver, counsel for EIN, said in an emailed statement, declining any further comment due to the pending case.

As Shahinian's lawsuit plodded through the legal system, he descended down its rabbit hole.

"Most people settle, but no one depended on this promise like I did, to this magnitude," Shahinian says. "There's no way I was gonna go down. I decided to fight it to the end."

He scoured the web for people associated with his lending deal.

He found his broker, who'd introduced himself as Bryan Stein, used different names and been indicted for financial crimes. The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office told NPR that the man, Boris Shteyngart, pleaded guilty in 2012 to grand larceny; public records show he served time in prison.

Shahinian spent a year tracking down some 700 business owners who'd been sued by EIN for debt collection.

Most did not want to revisit that chapter. Shahinian says that he connected with 70 and that many "came to tears" because "someone is standing up to bullies."

In the past decade, EIN has faced several lawsuits in at least nine states, records show. Most cases related to bankruptcies by its MCA borrowers, and most were settled or dismissed. In one case in Washington state, EIN was ordered to return the daily fees it continued to withdraw from a business that was already insolvent.

Last year, a U.S. district judge in Illinois ruled against EIN in a case over its 2019 MCA funding to a firm that federal regulators accuse of running a Ponzi-like scheme. The judge wrote that EIN "propped up" and "prolonged the Ponzi scheme" by either failing to conduct due diligence or ignoring its findings, and must return profits of $184,854.

Meanwhile in California, Shahinian's trial was delayed by another nine months. Shortly after, he lost his house to a foreclosure.

### A suspended reality

For 16 years, Shahinian lived in a lush suburban cul-de-sac in the vibrant Armenian American community of Glendale, north of downtown Los Angeles. In front of his former house is an ancient oak tree; the backyard spills onto the foot of a mountain.

At age 51, Shahinian sold off belongings, packed up his cats, computer screens, ticket printers and prized sound system — and moved in with his elderly parents.

Every dollar from the foreclosure sale, Shahinian says, went to pay mortgage debt and part of the debt to his best friend.

Several friends have urged him to move on from his costly seven-year legal fight, perhaps declare bankruptcy. To him, that's admitting defeat.

"My fault," he says, "was only believing in a promise that I could have never imagined to be false."

In recent years, a handful of states, including California, have started requiring MCA companies to be clearer, in writing, about their fees. And California recently also passed a law that, starting in 2028, will require funders and brokers to be licensed and undergo background checks and inspections.

It's too late for Shahinian.

His business is now back to basics: ticketing, mostly for local shows, and coding bells and whistles for his marketing software. He hopes his lawsuit will recoup more than $5 million — all the debt Shahinian estimates he has accrued since his "incident," including some $3 million in interest and fees.

He lays blame for its entirety at the feet of his funders, with a car-accident comparison. "You're being rear-ended," he says. "The 12-wheeler rear-ending you, you lose the steering wheel, and you smash into a bunch of cars, and everyone's focus is: Why did you smash into a bunch of cars?"

Heskin, Shahinian's lawyer, says the best-case scenario would be a multimillion-dollar judgment with punitive damages, "and then it's good luck collecting on it."

He's not sure what assets EIN or its employees named in Shahinian's lawsuit still have. NPR asked EIN's lawyers whether the firm still operates; they didn't respond. The firm's investors are unknown.

Shahinian argues any win would be meaningful.

"It would show everyone [whom] I affected these years that I'm in the right," he says. "Hopefully it would be a case for the industry to self-heal, self-correct. Maybe. And it'll be hope for others who are stuck — give them motivation."

"Don't give up, you know?" he says. "Don't be on path of least resistance. Go fighting."

He chuckles and pumps his fist up in the air.

NPR's Will Chase contributed to this report.

articles.title: How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
articles.author: Nicola Jones
articles.body_markdown:
This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”

El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. articles.title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
articles.author: Jane Arraf
articles.body_markdown:
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.

He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.

Now there are four.

A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.

Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.

The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.

"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."

He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.

"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.

Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.

Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.

It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.

### A test case

The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.

The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.

Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.

When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.

### Wrecked home

Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.

Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.

Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."

In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.

The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.

In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.

Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.

There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.

The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.

The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.

Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.

### Even the trees destroyed

Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.

"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."

Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.

Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.

"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.

Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.

Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.

"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.

She maintains a visceral connection to the land.

"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."

Villagers here feel abandoned by even their own government — and still in danger from nearby Israeli forces.

"Our homes were destroyed and no one came to check on us," Kadouh says. "Not the Lebanese state or outsiders or the parties," he says, referring to Hezbollah and its allies. "They just say 'Go back, go back' to the village. We came back and there are no essentials — no electricity, no water."

Kadouh has a son in the Lebanese army and another in national security services but he says, because the Lebanese army is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel, they have never been allowed to do their jobs.

"The Lebanese state never sent a soldier here to protect us," he says." That is why the parties and others came in — Hezbollah or Amal or even the Palestinian factions decades ago. "But the vacuum that the Lebanese state has left brought us to this tragedy" he says.

"We love the Lebanese army — let them bring us an army, but let them protect us," he says. "This army has a rifle — Israel has an F-35" fighter jet.

"But we would rather sit in the dirt," he says. "Our soul, our life is here, I was born here."

Kadouh says maybe someday there will be peace with Israel, but after all the deaths and destruction, not in his lifetime — and not with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Netanyahu is the one who killed my son. Let him bring back my son," he says. "If just yesterday Israel killed my son, am I supposed to tell the Israelis, 'Put your hand in my hand'? If they want to be our neighbors they should do good. Instead they burn us."

articles.author: Reece Rogers

Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

articles.title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.author: Lauren Sommer
articles.body_markdown:
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.

Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.

"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."

### Disagreements on fossil fuels

The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.

The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.

At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.

Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.

These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.

"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."

### Increasing electrification

This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.

Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas.

COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.

The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.

The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.

### Lack of U.S. Presence

The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.

An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.

### Billions of dollars still needed

While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.

Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.

"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."

In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.

As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035.

During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.

"Vulnerable countries from Africa and elsewhere are quite angry about that outcome," he says.

Earlier this year, countries requested $2.8 billion to help with damages, but only $342 million in funding was available.

At the COP31 summit, only $142 million in additional funding was pledged, far less than in other recent COP summits.

NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.

### Correction Nov. 22, 2026

A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.
